title: Possible Bruxism, Psychological Distress, and Knowledge of the Physiotherapist’s Role Among Health Sciences Students: A Cross-Sectional Study
content: Background/Objectives: Bruxism is a parafunctional habit characterized by clenching or grinding of the teeth. Anxiety, stress, and depression contribute to its etiology, and physiotherapists play an important role in its multidisciplinary management. This study aimed to analyze the association between bruxism and symptoms of anxiety, stress, and depression in university students, and to assess students’ knowledge of bruxism and of the physiotherapist’s role in its management. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 219 students, who completed an online questionnaire with three Oral Behaviors Checklist items (DC/TMD Axis II) and the 21-item Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21). Results: The median age was 22 years, and most participants were female (76.7%). The prevalence of possible bruxism was 60.3%. Stress was the predominant psychological profile (56.6%), followed by anxiety (24.3%). Possible bruxism was significantly associated with anxiety (p = 0.043) and stress (p = 0.018), but not with depression, lifestyle habits, or gender. Knowledge was associated with field and year of study (p < 0.05), being highest among dental medicine and physiotherapy students and senior students. Conclusions: Possible bruxism was highly prevalent in this student sample and was associated with anxiety and stress. These findings support early attention to psychological symptoms in this population.
